bib.title: Code Generation with AlphaCodium: From Prompt Engineering to Flow Engineering

legacy_report:
SOURCE: Code Generation with AlphaCodium: From Prompt Engineering to Flow Engineering. Tal Ridnik, Dedy Kredo, Itamar Friedman (CodiumAI). arXiv:2401.08500v1 [cs.LG], 16 Jan 2024. Preprint (no venue printed).
COVERAGE: 35190 of 35190 chars read, all pages including appendices A-D. The figures (flow diagram, token-count screenshots) were not viewed; the text around them was read. Scratch: /tmp/papers-t3/loop-2/alphacodium/t.txt

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Core: the AlphaCodium flow raises GPT-4 pass@5 on CodeContests validation from 19% (single direct prompt) to 44%.
  number: 19% -> 44%, x2.3
  setup: CodeContests validation set (107 problems); GPT-4; pass@5 = percent of problems solved using k=5 generated solutions per problem; baseline is "a single well-designed direct prompt".
  quote: "For GPT-4 on the validation set, for example, the pass@5 score improves from 19% to 44% - x2.3 improvement."
  where: Sec 5.1, p.7
- Gains hold across models and splits (Table 1, pass@5, direct prompt -> AlphaCodium):
  number: DeepSeek-33B val 7->20, test 12->24; GPT-3.5 val 15->25, test 8->17; GPT-4 val 19->44, test 12->29.
  setup: validation 107 problems, test 165 problems. Extraction flattens the table; the reading above is from the flattened text.
  quote: "GPT-4 validation Direct prompt 19%AlphaCodium 44% test Direct prompt 12%AlphaCodium 29%"
  where: Table 1, p.7
- Test-set gain is smaller than validation gain for GPT-4 (12% -> 29%, about x2.4 relative, +17 points vs +25 on validation).
  quote: same Table 1 line as above.
- Versus CodeChain (same model GPT-3.5, pass@5): AlphaCodium beats it on both splits.
  number: val 25% vs 17%; test 17% vs 14%.
  quote: "when comparing AlphaCodium to CodeChain with the same model (GPT-3.5) and the same metric (pass@5), AlphaCodium consistently does better."
  where: Sec 5.2, Table 2
- Versus AlphaCode (GPT-4, AlphaCodium pass@5):
  number: val 44% vs AlphaCode 17% (pass@10@1K) / 24% (pass@10@100K); test 29% vs 16% / 28%.
  quote: "Yet, the top results achieved by AlphaCodium are better"
  where: Sec 5.2, Table 2. Note the test-set margin over pass@10@100K is only 29% vs 28%. AlphaCode numbers are taken from its paper, not re-run.
- LLM call budget: about 15-20 LLM calls per solution, about 100 calls for pass@5.
  number: ~15-20 per solution; ~100 per pass@5; AlphaCode pass@10@100K = 1M calls (assumes one call per sample, which AlphaCode did not report), "four orders of magnitude" more.
  quote: "With AlphaCodium flow we perform ∼15-20 LLM calls per solution, so a pass@5 submission involves ∼ 100 LLM calls."
  where: Sec 5.3, p.7
- AlphaCode2 comparison: also four orders of magnitude more sample-efficient than AlphaCode, but it uses a heavily fine-tuned Gemini-Pro on an unreleased CodeContests variant. AlphaCodium uses general-purpose models as-is.
  quote: "AlphaCode2 requires about 100 samples to reach the level of performance of AlphaCode with a million samples, making it over 10000× more sample efficient."
  where: p.8
- Key design claim: generating extra tests is easier than generating a correct solution.
  quote: "A key observation when designing AlphaCodium flow is that generating additional useful tests is easier than generating a correct code solution."
  where: Sec 1, p.2; repeated in Sec 3.3
- Public tests vs AI tests: public tests are known correct, but "not comprehensive". Iterating on public tests alone "stabilizes and improves the solution but leaves 'blind spots'". AI tests (6-8 extra, aimed at cases the public tests miss, such as large inputs and edge cases) are then added. There is NO ablation table isolating the gain from public-test iteration vs AI-test iteration; Figure 1(b) is only an illustration.
  quote: "Generate an additional 6-8 diverse input-output tests for the problem. Try to cover cases and aspects not covered by the original public tests."
  where: Sec 3.2, Fig 1 caption
- Test anchors (guards against wrong AI tests). Iterate on the public tests first, and the passing ones become anchors. Then iterate on the AI tests one by one. A passing AI test joins the anchors. A failing AI test is assumed to mean the code is wrong, and the fix must also pass every anchor so far. AI tests are sorted easy to hard so anchors accumulate early.
  quote: "demand that the fixed code will also pass all the test anchors already acquired. As a result, the test anchors will protect us against an incorrectly fixed code."
  where: Sec 4, p.6
- Double validation: the model is asked to re-generate its own AI tests, correcting wrong outputs. The authors say this beats asking a yes/no "is this test correct?". There is no number for this.
  quote: "We found that this step of double validation, while encouraging the model to be critical and to reason, is more effective than asking a direct yes\no question"
  where: Sec 4, p.5
- Flow stages: problem reflection, public tests reasoning, 2-3 possible solutions, rank solutions, generate AI tests, initial code (retry until tests pass or a try limit; else keep the code with the closest output), iterate on public tests, iterate on AI tests. Stages can be merged into one call via YAML structured output.
  where: Sec 3.2-3.3
- Other practices (qualitative only, no ablation numbers): YAML structured output (preferred over JSON because of quoting and escaping, and fewer tokens), bullet-point reasoning, modular code (small sub-functions, which helps iterative fixing), postponing decisions and ranking several solutions instead of picking one, easy-to-hard accumulation of knowledge.
- Scorer is the private test suite: about 200 private input-output tests per problem, which the paper says keeps false positives down.
  quote: "each problem contains ∼200 private input-output tests the generated code solution must pass."
  where: Sec 2
- Distance-to-correct score for failed tests (Appendix D): used to pick the "closest output" code when none passes. A number gets L2 distance, a numeric array gets the sum of per-cell L2 distances, and a string array gets the count of non-identical cells.
- What did not work (Appendix C), with no numbers given: injecting the last 50 lines of the execution trace; injecting the last K failed solutions; injecting the last git patch diff; complicated single-stage prompts or non-iterative prompt chains.
  quote: "We have not observed improvement from this."
  where: App C, p.10

LIMITS
- Only CodeContests (validation 107 problems, test 165). Generality to other tasks is claimed as belief ("we believe"), not shown.
- pass@5 only. No variance, seeds, confidence intervals or cost in dollars. With 107 problems each point is about 1%.
- No component ablation table (reflection vs AI tests vs anchors etc.). The only comparison is direct prompt vs full flow, plus a qualitative Figure 1(b).
- AlphaCode and CodeChain figures are copied from their papers, because neither released reproducible scripts. The authors concede evaluation subtleties (multiple valid solutions, tolerance, timeouts). The AlphaCode call count is an assumption (1 call per sample). AlphaCode2 was evaluated on a different, unreleased benchmark variant.
- The "direct prompt" baseline is the authors' own design.
- Dated: models are GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and DeepSeek-33B as of 2024. The paper itself notes newer GPT versions have JSON mode. Possible contamination of CodeContests in the models is not discussed.
- Authors are from CodiumAI (commercial).

BUILDS ON: AlphaCode (Li et al. 2022, Science 378) as baseline and dataset; CodeContests (Li et al. 2022); CodeChain (Le et al. 2023) as comparison; AlphaCode2 (Gemini Team 2023); DeepSeek Coder (2023); chain-of-verification (Dhuliawala et al. 2023), self-consistency (Wang et al. 2022) and Nori et al. 2023 (Medprompt) cited as NL prompting techniques that did not transfer; HumanEval (Chen et al. 2021), APPS (Hendrycks et al. 2021) and MBPP (Austin et al. 2021) as the easier datasets.

CODE: No executable code. Figure 3 (p.6) is a YAML/Pydantic structured-output prompt for the possible-solutions stage:
"The output must be a YAML object equivalent to type $PossibleSolutions, according to the following Pydantic definitions: class Solution (BaseModel): name: str ... why_it_works ... complexity ..."
Repo: github.com/Codium-ai/AlphaCodium

FIGURES (from text only, not viewed)
- Fig 1(a), p.2: the flow. Pre-processing is reflection, public-test reasoning, solution generation and ranking, and AI test generation. The code iterations are initial code, iterate on public tests, then iterate on AI tests. This is the loop and scorekeeper structure.
- Fig 1(b), p.2: illustration of direct prompt, then public-test iteration (blind spots), then full flow.
- Fig 2, p.4: a CodeContests problem and an AI self-reflection on it.
- Fig 3, p.6: structured-output prompt.
- Fig 4, p.9: JSON vs YAML token counts.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Table 1 and Table 2 extracted with columns flattened (for example "Direct 7%AlphaCodium 20%"). The reading above is consistent with the abstract and text. Table 1's DeepSeek validation row says "Direct" and not "Direct prompt", which is a typo in the source.
